q: Do I recalculate my base year if I sell, close or buy a unit?
title: Base year after selling or buying a unit
short: Selling or buying a unit that existed in the base year is a structural change: recalculate the base year if the change passes your significance threshold. Closing a unit or opening a new one is organic decline or growth under the GHG Protocol, so the base year stays as it is.

ul: Sell a unit: remove its base year emissions from the base year.
Buy a unit that operated in the base year: add its base year emissions.
Move an activity in or out, such as handing forging to a vendor or taking packing back in house: adjust the base year for that activity.
Close a unit: no recalculation. The fall in emissions is real.
Build or open a new unit: no recalculation. Its emissions are growth.
Buy a unit that did not exist in the base year: no recalculation.

p: The GHG Protocol Corporate Standard, Chapter 5, asks you to set a threshold in advance and apply it every time. For validated targets, the SBTi's Corporate Near-Term Criteria require a recalculation policy with a threshold of 5% or less. Test each change on its own and all of a year's changes together against base year emissions.

ol: Get the unit's emissions for the base year, built with the same method and factors as yours: its bills and invoices if the seller hands them over, or a clearly labelled estimate.
Recalculate the base year for the full year, as if the new structure had applied all along.
Restate every year shown in your trend the same way, so the series compares like with like.
Keep the original figures and disclose the reason, the threshold and both totals.

sections.h: What a deal file should include
p: Ask the seller for twelve months of electricity bills and fuel invoices for the base year as part of due diligence. Without them, you will estimate a figure you then have to defend to buyers and lenders for years.

example.title: Illustrative year with a sale, a closure and a purchase
lines: Base year: 2,000 t CO2, of which Unit A 400 t and Unit B 100 t
Unit A sold: 400 / 2,000 = 20%, above 5%, so remove it
Unit B closed: organic decline, no change
Unit C bought, operating in the base year at 150 t: 150 / 2,000 = 7.5%, so add it
Restated base year: 2,000 minus 400 plus 150 = 1,750 t CO2
example.note: Figures are illustrative. 5% is the SBTi's ceiling; your written policy can set a lower threshold.

senseible: Senseible keeps each unit's invoices and bills with their dates and factors, so base year emissions for a unit can be taken out or added from documents rather than estimates. Records can be kept per plant or GSTIN.
